items.title: Learn to program using Python
items.text: This is a gentle introduction to the Python programming language. It assumes no prior programming experience and it aims to help you become fluent in the fundamentals. You will design, implement, test and debug real procedural programs, and will be able to read and reason about simple Python programs.

items.title: Learning outcomes
items.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  1. Write simple procedural programs.
  2. Read and analyze the behavior of simple programs.
  3. Apply decomposition — break a program into functions and modules.
  4. Choose appropriate data structures, conditionals, and iteration for a task.
  5. Use primitive types, variables, strings, expressions, and command-line I/O.
  6. Use conditional and iterative control structures, functions, and parameter passing.
  7. Use each of tuples, lists, sets, and dictionaries.
  8. Use the standard library.
  9. Use file I/O for persistence across runs.
  10. Test and debug simple programs.

items.title: A note on tools
items.text: You need almost nothing: a recent Python and any editor. We use the REPL (the interactive >>> prompt) constantly for quick checks, and script files for anything multi-line. The built-in help(), the official Python tutorial, and the interpreter's own error messages are the only references you will need.

items.title: Making decisions
items.text:
To be useful, programs often need to make decisions, that is, carry out certain actions based on whether certain conditions are met or not. This branching behavior stands on two legs:

  • Boolean expressions: Python expressions that produce a true or false value
  • Conditional logic: if and if-else statements. Decide whether to execute blocks of code based on the value of a boolean expression.

In this lesson we look at:

  • How to produce true or false values
  • How to test the value of a boolean expression using if statements
  • Code blocks and indentation in Python
  • How to write programs that behave differently based on input
  • More on string manipulation in Python, including string formatting

items.title: Booleans
items.text:
There are exactly two literal boolean values in Python: True and False.

However, a large number of Python expressions can evaluate to True or False.

items.title: Comparison
items.text:
Comparison operators are used to test equality (==), inequality (!=) and strict inequality (>, >=, <, <=):

>>> 3 == 3
True
>>> 3 < 3
False
>>> 5 >= 4
True
>>> 'apple' < 'banana'
True

= vs ==

= binds a variable to a value. E.g. x = 5

== compares two values for equality, return True if they are equal, and False otherwise.

Using = where == is expected is a very common error and Python will often flag it.

Comparing non-numeric values

You can compare things that are not numbers, such as strings or user-defined objects. This often requires supplying a comparison criterion or predicate.

By default, strings are compared alphabetically character by character. If you wanted to based the comparison on string length instead, then you would have to be explicit about it: len('apple') < len('banana')

items.title: Logical expressions
items.text:
You can combine multiple boolean expressions using the logical operators and, or and not to produce more complex expressions.

>>> True and True
True
>>> True and False
False
>>> True or False
True
>>> x = 3
>>> x > 0 and x <= 5
True
>>> 0 < x <= 5  # same as above
True
>>> not x > 5
True
>>> age = 25
>>> income = 40_000
>>> if age >= 18 and income > 30_000:   # BOTH must be true
...     print("eligible")
...
eligible
>>> day = "Sun"
>>> if day == "Sat" or day == "Sun":    # EITHER is enough
...     print("weekend")
...
weekend
>>> logged_in = False
>>> if not logged_in:                   # flip a boolean
...     print("please log in")
...
please log in

items.title: Truthiness
items.text:
Python allows you to use any value in conditional statements.

The following values are considered falsy:

  • zero: 0, 0.0
  • empty string
  • empty containers: [], (), {}
  • None

Everything else (non-zero numbers, non-empty strings, ...) are considered truthy.

>>> name = input("Please enter your name: ")
>>> Please enter your name: Ada
>>> if name:                                    # true if non-empty
...     print("Hi", name)
...
Ada
>>> items = []
>>> if not items:                               # same as `len(items) == 0` but cleaner
...     print("Empty")
...
Empty

items.title: Short-circuit evaluation
items.text:
Python stops evaluation logical expressions as soon as the final outcome can be determined. This allows some useful idioms:

  • Conditional execution without if statements: age < 18 and print("You are too young")
  • Default value assignment: user_name = user_input or 'Anonymous User'

  • Sentinel: guard against errors by ensuring a given operation is allowed. For example, the following code will produce an AttributeError if user is not set: 

    if not user.is_admin():
    print("Access denied")

    To prevent the AttributeError, ensure user is set:

    if user is not None and not user.is_admin():
    print("Access denied")

items.title: Other ways of getting booleans
items.text:
• is, the identity operator. Test if two variables reference the same object. Often used to test for None
  • Predicates:: functions or methods that return True or False. For example, string values have a method .isdigit() that returns True if all the characters in the string are digits, or False otherwise. Useful for testing valid user inputs. See More on strings

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
3.1 — Write sign.py that reads a number and prints positive, negative, or zero.

3.2 — Write login.py: read a username and password; grant access only if both match expected values (use and). Print distinct messages for wrong user vs. wrong password

3.3 — Write grade.py: read a score 0–100 and print the letter grade (A ≥ 90, B ≥ 80, C ≥ 70, D ≥ 60, else F). Also reject scores outside 0–100 with an error message.

3.4 — Write weekday.py: read a day name and print weekend or weekday. Accept any capitalization

3.5 — Write a program palindrome.py that prompts the user to enter a word and prints if it is a palindrome or not.

A palindrome is a word that reads the same when reversed.

Hints
  • 3.2 — nested if: outer if user == ...: then inner if password == ...:.
  • 3.4 — convert to lower case (.lower()) before comparing.
  • 3.5 — the expression [*word] converts word into a list of characters. The built-in function reversed() takes a sequence and returns its reverse. Then .join() the list of characters to form a new word.

items.title: Coding challenge — Number classifier program with a menu
items.text:
Write a menu-driven program classify.py as follows:

  1. Show a menu: 
    1) Classify a number
2) Check divisibility
3) Compare two numbers
  2. Read the user's choice with input().
  3. Branch on the choice:
  4. 1 — read a number; report whether it's positive/negative/zero and even/odd.
  5. 2 — read a number and a divisor; report whether the first is divisible by the second (n % d == 0), making sure to reject divisor 0 with an appropriate error message.
  6. 3 — read two numbers; report which is larger, or whether they're equal.
  7. If the choice isn't 1, 2, or 3, print Unknown option.
  8. Refuse to proceed on any invalid input

Exit program conditionally

It is often better to exit the program rather than proceeding with invalid input. You can do this conditionally using the built-in exit() function:

choice = input("Enter 1, 2 or 3: ")
if not choice.isdigit():
   exit(f"{choice!r} is not a valid number")
choice = int(choice)
if choice not in (1,2,3):
   exit(f"Unknown option {choice}")

items.title: If Statements
items.text: if statements let you branch out based on the outcome of a boolean test.

items.title: Code blocks
items.text:
Code blocks are a group of one or more statements that are meant to be executed as a unit. They are used to define the body of conditional statements, loops, functions and classes.

Python uses indentation to define code blocks and they have the following shape:

  • the block definition statement must end with a colon (:)
  • the block's body must be indented to the right by one space or more (4 spaces is the recommended amount). The indentation must be consistent for the entire block.
  • the block ends when the indentation returns to the previous level.

items.title: if — single branching
items.text:
Executes the block only if the test condition is True, and does nothing otherwise.

>>> temp = 32
>>> if temp > 30:
...    print("It's hot")
...    print("Drink water")
...
It's hot
Drint water

items.title: if - elif - else - multiple branching
items.text:
Evaluate multiple test conditions and execute the block of the first "true" branch. The else clause runs if no other branch evaluated to True.

>>> score = 75
>>> if score >= 90:
...    grade = "A"
... elif score >= 80:
...    grade = "B"
... elif score >= 70:
...    grade = "C"
... else:
...    grade = "F"
...
>>> print(grade) 
C

Order matters

Put the most specific / highest conditions first when there is overlap. In the previous example, if score >=70 were put first, everybody with a score greater than 70 would get a grade of "C", making the "A" and "B" grades unattainable!

items.title: Ternary operator
items.text:
You can use if - else to write expressions that return a value of any type based on a boolean expression

>>> height = int(input("Enter height in centimeters: "))
Enter height: 130
>>> "Tall" if height > 160 else "Short"
'Short'

items.title: Example
items.text:
# ticket.py
age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
if age < 0:
    print("Invalid age")
elif age < 5:
    print("Free")
elif age < 18 or age >= 65:
    print("Discounted: $8")
else:
    print("Full price: $12")

items.title: Testing facts about a string
items.text:
The str type in Python provides a variety of methods that test a given string for the presence of certain properties and return True or False. These methods can be useful in conditional expressions.

  • Check for the presence of a given prefix or set of prefixes or a given suffix or set of suffixes 
    >>> text = "the quick brown fox"
>>> text.startswith("a")
False
>>> text.startswith(("a", "the"))
True
>>> text.endswith("dog")
False
>>> text.endswith("x")
True
  • Predicates useful for input validation 
    >>> text = input("What is your age: ")
What is your age: 30
>>> text.isalpha()
False
>>> text.isalnum()
True
>>> text.isdigit()
True
>>> text.isnumeric()
True

items.title: Searching and replacing
items.text:
>>> text = "the quick brown fox"
>>> "quick" in text
True
>>> text.find("quick")
4
>>> text.find("lazy")
-1
>>> text.replace("quick", "lazy")
'the lazy brown fox'
>>> text.count("quick")
1

items.title: Splitting and joining
items.text:
>>> text = "\n      the quick brown fox"
>>> print(text)

    the quick brown fox
>>> text = text.strip()
>>> text.split()
['the', 'quick', 'brown', 'fox']
>>> text.split("quick")
['the', 'brown fox']
>>> '_'.join(text.split())
'the_quick_brown_fox'

items.title: f-strings
items.text:
It is common to build strings from values stored in variables. f-strings provide a convenient way to achieve this. 

>>> item = "oranges"
>>> price = 1.5
>>> quantity = 5
>>> print(f"You bought {quantity} {item}")
You bought 5 oranges
>>> print(f"Total: ${quantity * price:.2f}")
Total: $7.50

The :.2f in the previous example is a formatting specifier. It tells Python to format the value as a decimal number with two decimal places.

In addition to specifying the type and precision of a number, the Python formatting mini-language lets you customize other things such as width, alignment, padding, etc.

>>> amount = 50
>>> f"{amount:>5}"
'   50'
>>> f"{amount:<5}:
'50   '
>>> f"{amount:>5.2f}"
'50.00'
>>> f"{amount:*>5}"
'***50'
>>> f"{amount:*^5}"
'*50**'

items.title: Formatting columns of text
items.text:
# invoice.py
print("your invoice".upper().center(34))    # str also can center!
print()
print(f"{'Item':<10}{'Quantity':>9}{'Price':>6}{'Subtotal':>9}")
print("-" * 34)
print(f"{'Printer':<10}{1:>9}{45.99:>6.2f}{45.99:>9.2f}")
print(f"{'Cartridge':<10}{5:>9}{10.99:>6.2f}{5 * 10.99:>9.2f}")
print("-" * 34)
print(f"{f"${5 * 10.99 + 45.99}":>34}") # you can nest them!

           YOUR INVOICE

Item       Quantity Price Subtotal
----------------------------------
Printer           1 45.99    45.99
Cartridge         5 10.99    54.95
----------------------------------
                           $100.94

items.title: Getting Python
items.text: Before you can start writing programs, you need to install the Python interpreter on you machine.

items.title: Install Python
items.text:
You want Python 3.10 or newer (newer versions have friendlier error messages).

WindowsmacOSLinux

Get the Installer from the official Python website.

Add it to the system PATH

On the first installer screen, check "Add python.exe to PATH..

If you forget to do this, you will get an error when you try to run Python for the first time, and you will have to add it to the PATH manually.

brew install python, or use the installer from python.org

Python is almost certainly already there. Run python --version to check.

If not already installed, use your distro's package manager to install it.

Info

On some Linux distros, Python is invoked with python3 instead of python. Try which python and which python3 and if neither of those yields an answer, Python is probably not installed.

items.title: Install a code editor
items.text:
While you can write Python programs using any text editor, code editors provide a much better user experience. Some of the features you may want in a coded editor include:

  • Syntax highlighting: reveal the structure of your code using different colors
  • Automatic indentation: Python uses indentation as syntax and it is easy to forget or be inconsistent in how you indent your code. A good code editor takes care of that for you
  • Catch errors: you will make many mistakes while programming Python. A good code editor lets you know when that happens.

There are many code editors to choose from, but this course recommends Visual Studio Code from Microsoft. Get it from here: VS Code Download

Install Python extension in VS Code

In VS Code, go to Extensions tab, and search for "python". The official Microsoft Python extension is called ms-python.python. It has a Microsoft badge. Go ahead and install it.

The extension has features that makes it easier to write correct Python code. It should be pretty much the only extension you need.

items.title: Running Python
items.text: Python programs are instructions that are executed by an interpreter. The interpreter can be used interactively to execute instructions as you type them, or it can be used to execute instructions contained in a text file, a.k.a, a script.

items.title: The REPL — an interactive prompt for quick checks
items.text:
REPL stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop. It read Python expressions you type into it, evaluates them, prints the results to the screen and then waits for the next instruction.

Type python with no arguments into a terminal window. You will see these characters >>> printed on the screen, followed by a space. We call this a prompt and it is waiting for you to type something.

Try this:

>>> 2 + 3
5
>>> "hi" * 3
'hihihi'
>>> name = "Ada"
>>> name
'Ada'

Press Ctrl-D (macOS/Linux) or Ctrl-Z then Enter (Windows), or type exit(), to leave. Throughout the course, lines beginning with >>> mean "type this into the REPL" and the line under it is what the REPL echoes back.

items.title: Script files — for anything more than a line or two
items.text:
Real programs live in .py files. Create one and run it:

python3 hello.py

Where hello.py contains:

print("hello from a script")

hello from a script

Use print() if you want to see output from a script

The REPL evaluates what you type and prints the results immediately. A script does not - there you must call print(...) if you want to see output on the screen.

items.title: Create a home for your programs
items.text:
Make a folder for this course so nothing you try affects your existing files:

mkdir acit1515 && cd acit1515

Learn to use the terminal

mkdir and cd in the previous command create a folder and change into it respectively.

It is important to familiarize yourself with the terminal enough to be able to navigate the filesystem, create, open and delete files and folders and run commands. This is one of the first skills a programmer is expected to learn.

Also, learn where things are on your system. Make sure you know how to find where programs are installed, how to find your files, how to tell the type of a file - for example, Python scripts use the .py suffix. When you see such a file, you can immediately tell that it is a program intended to be processed by the Python interpreter. Similarly, when you see a .txt this tells you the file contains text, but it is not executable.

items.title: Getting help
items.text:
Python literally has a built-in help() function that exists to explain things. It doesn't explain everything, only things the interpreter knows. But it can be a quick way to look up information about Python language constructs and other Python objects.

Try this:

help(print)
help('while')       # for python keywords, surround them with quotes

For more detailed explanations, The Official Python Tutorial is a good place to start.

items.title: Exercises
items.text:
1.1 — Write about_me.py that prints three lines: your name, your city, and the number of programming languages you know (as a number, not text).

1.2 - Write the same program as above, but this time to this instead:

  • ask the user to enter their name and store this in a variable
  • ask the user to enter their city and store this in a variable
  • ask the user their favorite programming language and store this in a variable
  • print this information to the screen

1.3 — Predict, then run: what does each line print? 

print(5 * 3)
print("5" * 3)
print("5" + "3")
print(5 + 3, "apples")

1.4 — The following script has a bug. Read the traceback, say which error types it is, and fix it: 

print("Balance:" + 250)

1.5 — Use print to draw a small box exactly like this, using string repetition ("*" * n) — not by typing 10 stars by hand:

**********
*        *
**********

items.title: Homework
items.text: H1.1 — Write receipt.py that prints a mock receipt: a title line, a line of dashes made with string repetition, two item lines, and a total. Use print's multiple-argument form so numbers and text mix cleanly.

items.title: Input and Output
items.text: A useful program typically processes some input and produces output. Many programs manipulate text as both input and output.

items.title: print()
items.text:
In Python, the built-in print() function can be used to print text to the screen.

>>> print('Hello World')
Hello World
>>> print(5)
5

You can pass more than one value to the print() function; we call these arguments. When you do so, print() will output them with a space between them.

>>> print("x", "y", "z")
x y z
>>> print("total:", 3 + 4)
total: 7

Two useful keyword options:

>>> print("a", "b", sep="-")        # (sep = what goes between arguments)
a-b
>>> print("no newline", end="")     # won't print a newline
no newline

items.title: input()
items.text:
The built-in input() function is used to collect text typed by the user into a terminal and makes it available for the program to use. The input ends when the user presses ENTER.

>>> input('Please enter your name: ')
Please enter your name: Ada
'Ada'

You will always want to store the input into a variable before you can use it.

>>> name = input('Please enter your name: ')
Please enter your name: Ada
>>> print(name)
Ada

items.title: How Python runs your program
items.text:
A program is a list of statements the Python interpreter carries out in order, one after another:

print("first")
print("second")
print("third")

first
second
third

That top-to-bottom flow is the default and can only be changed by flow control statements and errors.

items.title: Comments
items.text:
Anything after # on a line is a comment. Python skips it entirely; it's there to explain why:

# Convert the price to cents to avoid rounding problems.
price_cents = 1999        # $19.99 stored as an integer number of cents

Good comments explain intent, not the obvious.

  • x = x + 1 # add one to x: not a very useful comment
  • x = x + 1 # advance to the next customer: this carries actual information

items.title: Strings and numbers are different kinds of thing
items.text:
"42" (with quotes) is text; 42 (no quotes) is a number. They behave differently

>>> print(2 + 3)
5
>>> print("2" + "3")
23

Mixing them is an error, and a very common one:

>>> print("age: " + 30)
...
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
>>> print("age: ", 30)
age: 30

items.title: Reading error messages
items.text:
When Python can't run something, it stops and prints a traceback. A traceback tells you what happened and where.

Always start reading from the bottom. That's where the most instructive information is.

# boom.py

print("start")
print(10 / 0)       # boom 
print("never runs")

start
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "boom.py", line 4, in <module>
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

  • ZeroDivisionError: division by zero — what went wrong.
  • File "boom.py", line 4 — where.
  • start printed, never runs did not — Python stopped at the error.

Here are some of the most common errors:

Error Means Typical cause SyntaxError Python can't even parse the line missing ), missing quote NameError a name isn't defined typo, or used before assigned TypeError wrong kind of value "age" + 30

items.title: Worked examples
items.text:
# greet.py — a first real script
print("What this program does: greets the world three ways.")
print("Hello, world!")
print("Hello,", "world!")            # print joins with a space
print("Hel" + "lo" + ", world!")     # strings joined by hand
print("=" * 20)                      # ⇒ ==================== (repeat a string)

What this program does: greets the world three ways.
Hello, world!
Hello, world!
Hello, world!
====================

items.title: Variables and data types
items.text:
Programs compute with values, remember them in variables, and combine them in expressions.

In this lesson, we look at:

  • rules of variables
  • how to work with text and numbers
  • some useful built-in functions

items.title: Converting between types
items.text:
Text from the keyboard (input()) always arrives as a string. To use user input in calculations, you must first convert it to numbers.

The built-in int() function takes a string, decimal or boolean (True or False) and tries to convert it into a integer.

float() does the same for decimals.

>>> year_of_birth = input("Please enter the year you were born: ")
Please enter the year you were born: 2006
>>> print("You were born", 2026 - int(year_of_birth), "years ago")
You were born 20 years ago

If int() is unable to convert the input, it produces a ValueError.

>>> int('abc')  # 'abc' does not represent any valid number in base-10
ValueError ...
>>> int('abc', 16)  # 'abc' is a valid hex number, i.e. base-16
2748
>>> int("3.5")  # does not allow a dot in the string. use `float()`
ValueError ...

Converting a decimal to an integer truncates the decimal part:

>>> int(3.5)
3

Python converts all operands of an arithmetic expression to float if any one operand is a decimal:

>>> 3 + 1.0
4.0

items.title: round() and abs()
items.text:
Use built-in round() to control the precision of decimal values:

>>> round(1 / 3)
0
>>> round(1 / 3, 2)
0.33

Use the built-in abs() to ensure a number is positive:

>>> abs(-7)
7
>>> abs(0.5)
0.5

items.title: ord and chr
items.text:
ord converts a character into its ASCII numeric value:

>>> ord('a')
97
>>> ord('A')
65

chr() converts in the opposite direction. So:

>>> print(chr(104) + chr(101) + chr(108) + chr(108) + chr(111))
hello

items.title: Examples
items.text:
# tip.py — split a restaurant bill
bill = 84.50
tip_rate = 0.18
people = 3

tip = bill * tip_rate           # 15.21
total = bill + tip              # 99.71
per_person = total / people     # 33.236666...

print("Tip:", tip)
print("Total:", total)
print("Each person pays:", per_person)
print("Rounded each:", round(per_person, 2))   # ⇒ 33.24  (round to 2 decimals)

# time_split.py — seconds into minutes and seconds, using // and %
seconds = 200
minutes = seconds // 60         # ⇒ 3
remaining = seconds % 60        # ⇒ 20
print(minutes, "min", remaining, "sec")     # ⇒ 3 min 20 sec

items.title: Excercises
items.text:
2.1 - Given the following restaurant bill:

  • bill: 84.50
  • tip rate: 0.18
  • Number of people: 3

Write a program (split-bill.py) that calculates how much each person will pay, rounding to 2 decimal points.

2.2 — A shop sells items at 4.75 each. Write a program (cost.py) that prompts the user to enter a quantity and stores it in a variable.

The program then computes the subtotal, adds 13% tax, and prints the subtotal, the tax, and the grand total, each rounded to 2 decimals.

2.3 — Write a program (temperature.py) that converts from Celsius to Fahrenheit using the following formulate: F = C * 9/5 + 32.

The program should prompt the user to enter degrees in Celsius, compute the conversion, and print both.

2.4 — Write a program (time-split.py) to convert a given number of minutes into hours and minutes. For example, 500 minutes would give 8 h 20 m. The program should prompt the user to enter the number of minutes, store it in a variable, compute the split and print the value the user entered and the result of the conversion.

2.5 — Write a program (number-swap.py) that swaps two variables. The program should prompt the user to enter the value for a and store it in a variable. Then prompt the user to enter the value for b and store it in a variable.

Then, using a single statement, swap the two variables.

Finally, print the "before" and "after" showing the values of a and b before and after the swap.

Hints
  • 2.2 — tax is subtotal * 0.13; grand total is subtotal + tax. round(x, 2).
  • 2.3 — write 9/5 (true division) not 9//5 (which is 1!). This is a classic bug.
  • 2.5 — use multi-variable assignment syntax.
  • Remember to convert user input to the appropriate type if used in calculations.

items.title: Homework
items.text:
H2.1 — Write change.py: given an integer number of cents (e.g. 287), print how many dollars and cents that is (2 dollars and 87 cents) using // and %.

The program should prompt the user for a number of cents above 100, store it in a variable, then compute the conversion and print the results.

H2.2 — Write powers.py that prints the first few powers of 2 (2**0 through 2**10). Use one print statement per line.

items.title: Numbers
items.text:
Numbers are one of the most useful data types in all of programming.

The two most commonly used number types are integers (int) and decimals (float).

Doing arithmetic:

>>> 7 + 2
9
>>> 7 - 2
5
>>> 7 * 2
14
>>> 7 / 2
3.5
>>> 7 // 2
3
>>> 7 % 2
1
>>> 7 ** 2
49

Division always produces a float

This is the case even in exact division:

>>> 10 / 2
5.0

n // m and n % m are complements of each other, and both produce integer results. The first produces the completed, whole part of the division. The other produces the remainder, or what's left over after the division.

0.1 + 0.2 is not equal to 0.3

Floating-point numbers cannot be represented exactly in Python.

Python always prints an approximation of the value stored by the machine. so, never compare two decimal values without rounding to the same decimal places first.

To learn more about this, read the Floating-point arithmetic module in the Official Python tutorial.

items.title: Precedence — the order of operations
items.text:
Python follows normal math order: ** first, then * / // %, then + -. Use parentheses whenever you're unsure or want to be clear:

>>> 2 + 3 * 4
14
>>> (2 + 3) * 4
20
>>> 2 ** 3 ** 2
512

Grouping is right-to-left

The last expression in the previous example may be surprising. ** groups right-to-left, meaning 3**2 is evaluated first.

When in doubt, parenthesize.

items.title: Strings
items.text:
In Python the type used to represent text is called string. You can use strings to provide feedback to the user during program execution or output logs from the program.

You can generate strings from other strings:

>>> firstname = "Ada"
>>> lastname = "Lovelace"
>>> fullname = firstname + " " + lastname
>>> print(fullname)
Ada Lovelace

You can convert most types to strings:

>>> age = str(25)
>>> print("You are " + age + " years old")
You are 25 years old

Without the str(25) conversion, the print() statement would have produced a TypeError.

Other ways to concatenate (join) strings:

>>> 'Hello' ' world'
'Hello world'
>>> ('Hello'
... ' world')
'Hello world'

Use pairs of triple single or double quotes for multi-line strings:

>>> html = """
<body>
    <h1>About</h1>
</body>
"""

Suppressing newline character in multi-line strings

When printed, the html variable will output a newline character at both ends of the string.

This is often not what you want. Use a \ to suppress a newline character anywhere in the string.

>>> html = """\
... <body>
...     <h1>About</h1>
... </body>"""

The special \ character is used to escape special characters such as quotes, non-printable characters and other characters that have meaning in the language (such as parentheses, braces, brackets, ...).

>>> "\"Watch out!\" she cried"
'"Watch out!" she cried'

Raw strings

There are times when you need to output the literal \. You can handle this in two ways:

  • escape the \: path="C:\\Program files\\Python314"
  • use raw strings: path=r"C:\Program files\Python314"

Uppercase and lowercase:

>>> 'python'.upper()
'PYTHON'
>>> 'PYTHON'.lower()
'python'

Get part of a string:

>>> lang = 'python'
>>> lang[0].upper + lang[1:]
'Python'
>>> lang[:-1] + lang[-1].upper()
'pythoN'

Indexing and slicing

lang[0] in the previous example is called indexing. This means retrieving the character at the given position in the string. Strings are sequences and their indexes start from 0.

The expression var[n:m] is called slicing. This means retrieving a substring starting at position n (inclusive) up to position m (exclusive).

Negative index values are permitted and they start at the end of the string.

items.title: Variables
items.text:
A variable is a name bound to a value with = (assignment). Read x = 5 as "let the name x refer to 5," not "x equals 5".

>>> price = 20
>>> quantity = 3
>>> total = price * quantity
>>> print(total)
60

A variable can be rebound, that is, it can be made to point to a different value, potentially of a different type.

>>> n = 10
>>> n = n + 1
>>> print(n)
11
>>> n = "now text"
>>> print(n)
now text

Right side first

In n = n + 1, Python evaluates n + 1 first, using the current value of n then makes n refer to the result. That is, the right hand side of an assignment statement is always evaluated first.

The value cannot be on the left-hand side of an assignment statement

The following is illegal in Python:

10 = n

The left-hand side of an assignment statement must always be an identifier, a.k.a variable name.

items.title: Naming rules & style
items.text:
• use letters, digits, and underscores
  • a variable name cannot start with a digit
  • variable names are case-sensitive (total and Total are different names)
  • style: lowercase with_underscores
  • style: descriptive. Prefer tax_rate over tr

items.title: Assignment shortcuts
items.text:
Multiple assignments on one line:

>>> x, y = 1, 2
>>> a = b = 0

Update and rebind:

>>> count = 0
>>> count += 5
>>> count -= 2
>>> print(count)
3
